evals.prompt: I've got two brand colours, #1e3a8a and #fbbf24. Build me a full 50-950 colour scale that runs through both, as CSS custom properties I can drop straight into our design system. Name them --brand-*.
evals.expected_output: The bundled script is run with an 11-step Tailwind-style ramp in CSS format named `brand`, emitting a `:root` block of `--brand-50 ... --brand-950` in which both input colours appear unmodified (--brand-400 is #1e3a8a, --brand-900 is #fbbf24).
evals.setup: color-ramp is model-invoked. Run it in a scratch directory. Grade the emitted CSS and the transcript of how it was produced.
expectations: The transcript shows the bundled script (scripts/generate_scale.py) being executed — the scale is NOT computed by hand-writing OKLCH, hex-conversion, or interpolation maths in the response.
Output is a CSS `:root { ... }` block of custom properties whose prefix is `--brand-`.
Exactly 11 tokens are emitted, labelled 50, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900, 950.
Both input colours appear exactly as token values: one token is `#1e3a8a` and another is `#fbbf24`.
Lightness increases monotonically from --brand-50 (darkest) to --brand-950 (lightest) — no step is darker than the one before it.
`--steps 11` was chosen because the user asked for a 50-950 ramp, and `--format css` / `--name brand` because they asked for CSS custom properties named --brand-* (judgement).

evals.prompt: Give me a 9-step scale from navy to gold so I can eyeball whether it actually works.
evals.expected_output: The two named colours are resolved to concrete hex first (confirming if genuinely ambiguous), then the script is run to produce a 9-step dark-to-light scale in a format meant for visual inspection (html swatch preview or table), with both resolved anchors present exactly.
evals.setup: color-ramp is model-invoked. If the resolved hex for 'navy'/'gold' is ambiguous the skill may confirm; supply a reasonable choice (e.g. navy ~#000080, gold ~#ffd700) so the run can proceed. Grade the resulting scale and the transcript.
expectations: The named colours navy and gold are resolved to specific 6-digit hex codes before the scale is generated (judgement).
The transcript shows scripts/generate_scale.py being run — the scale is not derived by hand.
The scale has exactly 9 steps, ordered dark to light.
A visual/scannable format is chosen for 'eyeball' — html swatch preview or table — rather than raw json (judgement).
Both resolved anchor colours appear exactly in the output and are marked as the two anchors.
If html is produced, the file is presented or its path surfaced so the user can open it; if table, it is shown inline (judgement).

evals.prompt: That scale you just made is still too washed out through the middle — make it more vivid.
evals.expected_output: The script is re-run with a raised --chroma-boost (roughly 0.6-0.8) rather than the individual hex values being hand-edited, and both anchor colours still appear exactly in the new output.
evals.setup: Two-turn scenario. Prior turn: the user asked for a scale through #10b981 and #f472b6 and the skill ran generate_scale.py at the default --chroma-boost 0.45. This prompt is the follow-up complaint. Grade the follow-up behaviour and its output.
evals.note: This targets the skill's tuning loop: complaints about washed-out/muddy results are answered by re-running with a different --chroma-boost, never by manually rewriting hex values.
expectations: scripts/generate_scale.py is re-run with --chroma-boost raised above the previous value (roughly 0.6-0.8).
The individual hex values from the previous output are NOT hand-edited — the new scale comes from re-running the script, as shown in the transcript.
Both input colours (#10b981 and #f472b6) still appear exactly in the regenerated scale.
The response attributes the increased vividness to the raised chroma-boost, not to manual colour picking (judgement).

evals.prompt: I need a 5-step palette between #222222 and #dddddd as JSON so I can feed it into our token pipeline.
evals.expected_output: The script is run with --steps 5 --format json, emitting a valid JSON array of 5 step objects in which both #222222 and #dddddd are present with a non-null anchor field, passed through verbatim rather than reformatted by hand.
evals.setup: color-ramp is model-invoked. Run in a scratch directory. Grade the emitted JSON and the transcript.
expectations: The transcript shows scripts/generate_scale.py being run with --format json and --steps 5.
The output parses as valid JSON: an array of exactly 5 objects, each carrying hex, label, and anchor fields.
Both #222222 and #dddddd appear as hex values in the array, and their objects have a non-null anchor value ("A" or "B").
The 5 steps run dark to light with monotonically increasing lightness.
The JSON handed back is the script's own output, not re-serialised or edited by hand (judgement).

evals.prompt: We're standardising our design tokens. Can you take #0b1e3f and #e8c07d and give me a dark-to-light set of shades that includes both of those exact colours? CSS variables ideally.
evals.expected_output: The color-ramp skill fires on its own — the user never names it — because the request gives two hex colours and asks for a dark-to-light scale through both as CSS design tokens, which is exactly what the description covers.
evals.setup: Triggering test. Present this prompt to an agent that has the color-ramp skill available among its skills but is NOT told which skill to use. Judge only whether color-ramp is selected and invoked; the quality of the resulting scale is out of scope here.
evals.note: Tests the description's model-invocation, not execution. The cues that should fire it: two hex anchors + 'dark-to-light set of shades that includes both' + 'CSS variables' / 'design tokens'.
expectations: The color-ramp skill is invoked in response to this prompt, without the user naming the skill or its script.
The skill is selected on the strength of the matching cues — two hex colours and a scale/tokens request through both — rather than by coincidence (judgement).

evals.prompt: Give me a set of lighter and darker shades of #3b82f6 for our button hover and active states.
evals.expected_output: The color-ramp skill does NOT fire — the request gives only one colour, and the skill is for a scale running through TWO anchor colours. The agent handles the single-colour tint/shade request without invoking color-ramp.
evals.setup: Negative triggering test. Present this prompt to an agent that has the color-ramp skill available but is not told which skill to use. Judge only whether color-ramp is (correctly) NOT invoked.
evals.note: Guards against over-triggering on the words 'shades'/'lighter'/'darker'. The load-bearing distinction is the anchor count: color-ramp needs two colours; this prompt supplies one.
expectations: The color-ramp skill is NOT invoked for this prompt.
The agent recognises that only one colour was given, so a two-anchor scale skill does not apply (judgement).
